Early Roots and the Search for Belonging.
Every story has its beginning, right? And for some people, that starting point isn’t just a place or a date—it's a nagging question that sticks around for years: Where do I actually fit in?
Picture this—a boy growing up in the California suburbs, in a modest home filled with the buzz of fresh ideas, but also a quiet ache that he just didn’t quite belong. He was adopted as a baby. And even though his parents gave him all the love and care they could, there was still that mark left by knowing he’d been given up by his birth parents.
If you’ve ever wondered whether you truly belong—or if you’re just a guest in someone else’s story—you know exactly what that feels like.
Now, this boy, smart and restless, couldn’t help but be drawn to the world of gadgets and wires. His dad was the kind of person who worked with his hands, and he loved showing his son how to pull things apart and put them back together again. Those long hours together in the garage, surrounded by the smell of oil and the clatter of tools, taught him more than just how things worked—they taught him the magic of making something come alive with your own hands.
Most people don’t realize, but so much of true innovation actually starts with tinkering—with just being willing to break things and see what happens.
But if the garage was where he thrived, school was a different story. The classroom felt like a cage, the lessons just didn’t spark his curiosity. He was that student—the one who challenged teachers, questioned rules, and sometimes pushed things just a little too far.
There’s a special kind of energy in people who can’t settle for the way things are. Sometimes it’s a gift, sometimes it’s a burden. For him, it meant a lot of boredom and frustration—but it also gave him this deep drive to find something more meaningful.
As the years went on, the world around him started shifting. California in the ‘60s and ‘70s was buzzing with rebellion and reinvention. New ideas about technology, art, even how to live, were in the air. And he found himself right in the middle of it—drawn to the counterculture and to people who truly believed life could be different if you were just bold enough to imagine it.
He started exploring all kinds of new ways of thinking—from Eastern philosophies to alternative diets—always searching for a purpose that felt real.
Then, in high school, he met someone who would change everything for him—a quiet, brilliant mind who loved electronics just as much. They spent hours building little gadgets together, always dreaming bigger. Their partnership was powered by this shared belief that two people in a garage could actually change the world.
It’s funny, isn’t it? Some of the most world-changing ideas don’t come from fancy boardrooms—they start in garages, in the hands of people who just refuse to settle for “good enough.”
Throughout it all, his search for belonging, for a place to call home, shaped every single decision. It’s what pushed him to question, to create, and to keep moving, even when the path ahead looked uncertain.
For some folks, that need to prove themselves never really goes away. It becomes the engine that drives them to do what others think is impossible.
